## 1. Conduct a permutation test

Conduct a permutation test to investigate the following question:

> Do homes built pre-1970 have higher average lead soil concentrations?

To perform this test, you'll need the `exide-property-covariates.csv` file found in `/courses/EDS222/data`. This file contains the year each property was built.

::: {.callout-note}

The question is about _average lead soil concentrations_. You'll need to first get the average lead soil concentration for each property, then join your result to the property covariate data to get the year the house was built.


N0 = Homes built pre-1970 do not have a higher in average lead soil concentration than homes built after 1970. 
N1 = Homes built pre-1970 have a higher average lead soil concentration than homes built after 1970. 

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(222)
soil <- read.csv('data/exide-soil-cores.csv')
properties <- read.csv('data/exide-property-covariates.csv')

# Remove NAs from prop
properties <- properties |> 
    drop_na(year_built)
```
:::

```{r}
# Find the means of the lead concentrations per property
meanbyprop <- soil |> 
    summarize(meanpbppm = mean(pb_ppm, na.rm=TRUE), .by=property_id)
```

```{r}
# Join the data frames
soil_cores <- left_join(properties, meanbyprop, by= join_by(property_id)) 

```



```{r}
# Add a pre1970 column to soil_cores
soil_cores <- soil_cores |> 
    mutate(pre1970 = year_built < 1970)
```

```{r}
# Visualize the raw data by plotting houses built pre and post 1970, and the mean pb ppm. 
soil_cores |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=as.factor(pre1970), y=meanpbppm))+
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_x_discrete(
    name="",labels = c("FALSE" = "Post 1970", "TRUE" = "Pre 1970")

  )

```
```{r}
# Find the mean lead levels in soil before and after 1970 using new pre1970 column. 
soilmeansprepost <- soil_cores |>
  summarize(meanprepost = mean(meanpbppm), .by = pre1970) |>
  arrange(pre1970)
```

```{r}
# Find the difference in means between the mean lead levels in the soil before and after 1970. 
observeddifmean <- soilmeansprepost$meanprepost[2]-soilmeansprepost$meanprepost[1]
```

```{r}
# Now shuffle the samples and do it again 
 shuffled_year <- soil_cores |>
      mutate(pre1970 = sample(pre1970)) |>
      summarize(meanprepost = mean(meanpbppm), .by = pre1970)
```

```{r}
# Find the difference in means of the shuffled samples. 
shuffledifmean <- shuffled_year$meanprepost[2] - shuffled_year$meanprepost[1]
```

```{r}
# Now repeat shuffling the samples and finding the difference in means 10,000 times.
prepost_null_dist <- replicate(
  1e4,
  {
    shuffled_year <- soil_cores |>
      mutate(pre1970 = sample(pre1970)) |>
      summarize(meanprepost = mean(meanpbppm), .by = pre1970)
    shuffled_year$meanprepost[2] - shuffled_year$meanprepost[1]

  } )
```

```{r}
# Plot the null distribution.
tibble(diff_means=prepost_null_dist) |>
  ggplot(aes(prepost_null_dist)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5)
```

```{r}
# Create the p value.
pval <- mean(prepost_null_dist>observeddifmean)

```
```{r}
## The p value of this permutation test was 0, which is below an alpha of 0.05. This means that we have evidence to reject the null hypothesis that houses built pre-1970 do not have higher soil lead concentrations than houses built after 1970. This means that the probaility of observing our sample if the null is true is close to 0. 

```

## 2. Estimate a confidence interval

Estimate a confidence interval to investigate the following question:
```{r}
# Create a column for distance to freeway in kilometers.
soil_cores <- soil_cores |> 
  mutate(dist_to_freeway_km=dist_to_freeway_m / 1000) |> 
    mutate(close = dist_to_freeway_km <= 1)

```


```{r}
# Visualize the raw data by plotting the distance to freeway and the mean pb ppm. 
soil_cores |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=as.factor(close), y=meanpbppm))+
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_x_discrete(
    name="",labels = c("FALSE" = "Further than 1 km", "TRUE" = "Within 1 km")

  )

```

> How much is the difference in average lead soil concentrations between properties within 1km of a freeway and those farther away?

```{r}
# Find the mean in pb ppm by if samples were taken closer or further from 1 km from a freeway.
dist_observed <- soil_cores |>
  summarize(dist_to_freeway_mean_obs = mean(meanpbppm), .by = close) |>
  arrange(close)
```

```{r}
# Find the difference between samples taken close and far.
dist_observed_diff = dist_observed$dist_to_freeway_mean_obs[2]-dist_observed$dist_to_freeway_mean_obs[1]
```
```{r}
# Now repeat the above process 10,000 times.  

area_samp_dist <- replicate(
  1e4,
  {
    resampled <- soil_cores |>
      slice_sample(n = nrow(soil_cores), replace = TRUE) |>
      summarize(dist_to_freeway = mean(meanpbppm), .by = close) |>
      arrange(close)

    resampled$dist_to_freeway[2] -
      resampled$dist_to_freeway[1]
  }
)

```

```{r}
# Find the 95% conf int
area_95ci <- quantile(area_samp_dist, c(0.025, 0.975))
```

```{r}
# Plot the distribution
tibble(diff_means = area_samp_dist) |>
  ggplot(aes(diff_means)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1)  +
  geom_vline(xintercept = dist_observed_diff, color = "magenta", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = area_95ci, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.5)
```

```{r}
# According to this confidence interval, we are 95% confident that the true population difference in means in lead concentrations between houses within a kilometer of the freeway and without lies between 39 and 102 ppm. 
```


## 3. Simulate a negative result

Recall that a p-value is the probability of observing your sample _if_ the null hypothesis is true. Therefore, if you draw a sample from two groups that part of the same population, you should get a p values less than 0.05 only 5% of the time. In other words, a negative result (no actual difference) will yield a significant p-value at the 0.05 threshold in 5% of samples. This is known as the **false positive rate**.

To simulate a negative result, perform the following.

1. Define a normally-distributed population. Pick any mean and standard deviation.
2. Draw a sample of 50 observations from this population. Assign the first 25 to group A and the second 25 to group B.
3. Conduct a permutation test to investigate whether the mean of group A is greater than the mean of group B.
4. Record your p-value.
5. Repeat the simulation 1,000 times.

When you're done, verify that your p-value is less than 0.05 in approximately 5% (50) of your simulations.

```{r}
# Create a population with a random mean and SD 
 normaldistpop <- rnorm(50, mean = 23, sd = 8)
 ```
## Choose parameters for this simulation 

```{r}
# Create groups that each contain half of the population
group1 <- normaldistpop[1:25]
group2 <- normaldistpop[26:50]


obsdif = mean(group1) - mean(group2)


```

```{r} 
# Permutation test

# Combine and shuffle the two groups, and then divide them up again
combine_groups <-c(group1, group2)
shuffled1 <- combine_groups[1:25]
shuffled2 <- combine_groups[26:50]
 
 # Shuffle and pull from each group, 
 # calculcate the mean of each group, 
 # and find the dif in means - 1e4 times.
 diffmeans <- replicate( 1e4 ,{
 shuffled <- sample(combine_groups)
 samplegroup1 <- shuffled[1:25]
 samplegroup2 <- shuffled[26:50]

 firstmean <- mean(samplegroup1)
 secondmean <- mean(samplegroup2)

 sampdiff <- mean(samplegroup1) - mean(samplegroup2)
 sampdiff
 }
 )
 # Find p value by taking the mean of how often the shuffled means are greater than observed mean
pval <- mean(diffmeans>obsdif)
```

```{r} 
# Create a function out of permutation test so that we can call it 1000 times.
simulation <- function() {
normaldistpop <- rnorm(50, mean = 23, sd = 8)
  group1 <- normaldistpop[1:25]
group2 <- normaldistpop[26:50]


obsdif = mean(group1) - mean(group2)

 combine_groups <-c(group1, group2)
 
 diffmeans <- replicate( 1e4 ,{
 shuffled <- sample(combine_groups)
 samplegroup1 <- shuffled[1:25]
 samplegroup2 <- shuffled[26:50]

 firstmean <- mean(samplegroup1)
 secondmean <- mean(samplegroup2)

 sampdiff <- mean(samplegroup1) - mean(samplegroup2)
 sampdiff
 }
 )
pval <- mean(diffmeans>obsdif)

return(pval)
}

```

```{r}
# Create the distribution of all 1000 p values
pval_dist <- replicate(1000, simulation())
```

```{r}
# Graph distribution of p-values
pvals <- tibble(pvaldist = pval_dist) |>
ggplot(aes(pvaldist)) +
geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.02) +
geom_vline(xintercept = 0.05, linewidth = 1)

pvals




```

```{r}
# Find the proportion of p values that show statistical significance
mean(pval_dist <= 0.05)
```

There is no difference in means in this test, since we are pulling randomly from two identical groups. This test shows that the frequency of getting a false positive (incorrectly being able to reject the null that there is no difference) is about 5%.
